title: India in Space: From Thumba to the Lunar South Pole
subtitle: Six decades of the Indian space programme in one page: what it has done, how it launches, and what comes next.
summary: A design demonstration built from widely published public-record facts. It shows how a Hermes research result becomes a readable briefing; it is not a BIGDATA research output.
author: Prepared with Hermes

points: India has moved from launching borrowed sounding rockets in 1963 to soft-landing near the Moon's south pole in 2023.
Three domestic launch vehicles now cover small, medium and heavy payloads, so most national missions launch from Indian soil.
The next phase is human spaceflight (Gaganyaan) and a national space station, alongside a fast-growing private launch sector.

items.label: Country to soft-land on the Moon

sections.title: From sounding rockets to the Moon
sections.lede: The programme grew in deliberate steps: first rockets, then satellites, then the vehicles to launch them, then deep space.

sections.title: Building capability one step at a time
sections.body:
India's first rocket launch, a small sounding rocket, lifted off from Thumba near Thiruvananthapuram in November 1963. The site was chosen because it lies close to the magnetic equator, which made it valuable for upper-atmosphere research.

The first Indian satellite, Aryabhata, followed in 1975 on a Soviet launcher. Five years later the SLV-3 rocket placed the Rohini satellite in orbit, making India a nation able to launch its own satellites.

The decades since have been spent on reliable launchers and application satellites for communications, weather and Earth observation, before turning outward to the Moon, Mars and the Sun.
sections.pullquote: Each step was built on the one before: rockets, then satellites, then launchers, then deep space.

sections.title: Milestones
sections.intro: Selected missions, in order. Dashed markers are planned, not yet flown.

events.title: First rocket launch from Thumba
events.body: A sounding rocket opens India's launch history.

events.title: Aryabhata
events.body: India's first satellite, launched by the Soviet Union.

events.title: SLV-3 orbits Rohini
events.body: First satellite placed in orbit by an Indian rocket.

events.title: Chandrayaan-1
events.body: First lunar mission; its instruments contributed to the detection of water molecules on the Moon.

events.title: Mars Orbiter Mission reaches Mars
events.body: Orbit achieved on the first attempt.

events.title: PSLV-C37: 104 satellites
events.body: A record number of satellites deployed by one rocket at the time.

events.title: Chandrayaan-3 lands
events.body: First soft landing near the lunar south pole.

events.title: Aditya-L1 launched
events.body: Solar observatory sent towards the Sun-Earth L1 point.

events.title: SpaDeX docking
events.body: Two satellites dock in orbit, a key step for a future station.

events.title: Gaganyaan crewed flight
events.body: India's first human spaceflight on a domestic rocket.

sections.title: How India launches
sections.lede: Three operational rockets cover most national needs; the heaviest also carries the human spaceflight programme.

sides.name: PSLV
points: Optimised for polar and sun-synchronous orbits
Carried Chandrayaan-1 and the Mars Orbiter Mission

sides.name: GSLV Mk II
points: Places communication and navigation satellites in transfer orbit
Uses an Indian-built cryogenic upper stage

sides.name: LVM3
points: A human-rated version is planned for Gaganyaan

items.title: Human spaceflight
items.body: Gaganyaan aims to fly Indian astronauts on an Indian rocket; uncrewed test flights come first.

items.title: A national space station
items.body: Plans for a Bharatiya Antariksh Station build on the SpaDeX docking demonstration.

items.title: Lunar sample return
items.body: Chandrayaan-4 is planned to bring lunar samples back to Earth.

items.title: Private launchers
items.body: Indian start-ups have begun flying their own rockets since the sector opened to private firms.

sections.title: Assessment
sections.body: The programme's strength is steady, low-cost progress: each mission reuses proven hardware and adds one new capability. The main risks to the next phase are schedule, since human spaceflight carries far stricter safety demands, and the pace at which industry can take over routine launches.
